tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/port-hack

# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Before copying anything, read `techniques.md` and every file in
`.claude/rules/` (`hacks.md`, `x11shim.md`, `device-display.md`, `gl.md`,
`tools-scoring.md`) in full. The gotchas live there, and a harness may not load
them for you (`.pi/rules` links to the same directory for pi).

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Xft text (`XftDrawStringUtf8`) | Xft text (XJack) |
| Threads, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

## 4. Verify on the host

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. For a
single-precision wrapper, also build for the device and run
`uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>`: a count in a per-frame function is
a literal, macro or struct the rename missed (`techniques.md`). Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, marking anything unmeasured as such. After a
batch, log one 20 s-a-hack rotation lap and run `tools/triage_hacks.py`
(`hacks.md` says how): it shows which hacks are step-bound, push-bound or paced
by their own delay, with their soft-double calls, so a slow hack is looked at
for the right reason.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Done means

A port is done on the host only when all of these hold: a dumped frame viewed
at two or more frame counts (with seeds forced if the hack picks a mode); a
leak test, mutation-checked; the largest stack frame measured; the hash pinned
from a frame you looked at; and a notices row that matches each file's header.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It is rated S, so I need not read it" | Maze was rated L for Xlib gaps; the real blocker was a 20 MB `calloc`. |
| "It compiles, so it works" | Rorschach compiled and rebooted on its first frame. |
| "The colours look right" | Not from a host frame: every hack was byte swapped until Maze. |
| "My test passes, so it tests something" | A test through Pyro passed with the runner broken. Break the code on purpose. |
| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |
| "Single precision is done, so the hack is as fast as it gets" | HexTrail gained 0.3 fps from it and 2.3 from a depth clear in the GL layer. Read what the shared code does each frame. |
| "The mean is above 10 fps" | HexTrail's mean was 15.3 and its worst window 10.8; its step grew all cycle. Read the lowest window. |
| "Dump with 0 and 5 frames exits cleanly, so it works" | That shows it starts and stops, not what it draws. Convert a frame to PNG and look. |
| "A `0` in `kBaseline` keeps the suite green" | It also stops the suite checking a single frame. Use `0x1ull` until you have looked, then pin. |
| "A hook will not run, so `--no-verify`" | That skips ruff, markdownlint and gitleaks. `SKIP=<hook>`, and say so in the PR. |

# Flashing and measuring on the device

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build. Unescaped quotes fail
  with "error: 'truchet' was not declared in this scope".
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod" over
  "Begbie"; `\n` starts a new line). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  `-DQR_URL=\"https://example.com\"` sets the QR overlay's target (default the
  LinkedIn profile). Check it reached the binary with
  `strings -a .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c 'example.com'`.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- Serial log: `.venv/bin/python -I tools/serial_capture.py <out-file>
  <seconds> [port]` reads `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 into a file and
  reopens the port when it goes away. Run it in the background with absolute
  paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= sync= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack,
  the push, the wait for the panel's TE edge before a synced push (only
  Unknown Pleasures; not counted in `push=`) and the wait; mean canvas rows
  sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
  `serial_capture.py` sets `dtr` and `rts` to False on an unopened
  `serial.Serial()` before `open()`, as any script of your own must: a reopen
  loop without that once parked the chip in its bootloader
  (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen). Recover, or reset just
  before a capture to log from boot (a hack's `fprintf(stderr)` reaches the
  log), with `.venv/bin/python .platformio/packages/tool-esptoolpy/esptool.py
  --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 --after hard_reset read_mac`.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `ad-flyingtoasters` force flags (add to `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS`):
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_ART=0|1` (0 is 1-bit, 1 is colour) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_DONENESS=0|1|2` (light, medium, dark) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1|2` (2 is the default, with 6 flyers; 1 is the
  original size, with 10); a number outside those is an `#error`. It logs
  `ad-flyingtoasters: <art>, doneness=<level>` to stderr at start.
- To see where a GL hack's frame goes, add `-DGL_PROFILE`: a `glprof` line
  follows each `run` line with time per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill). Time left
  over is the hack's own code. To compare builds, `.venv/bin/python -I
  tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 --out <dir>
  "a=-DGL_PROFILE" "b=-DGL_PROFILE -DFOO"` builds each variant pinned, flashes
  them in turn and tabulates the windows. It flashes: run it only with Rod's
  go-ahead. It builds each hack's variants from the working tree when that
  hack's turn starts, so leave `src/` and `tools/tinygl_patch.py` alone until
  the last hack has built. It compares flag variants of one tree: to A/B a
  change, put it behind a temporary `-D` switch (as `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` does).
  It takes one `--hack` per run: loop several from a scratchpad script run
  with `run_in_background`, and `touch` a done file at the end.
- `-DDCACHE_LINE32` keeps the SDK's 32-byte data-cache lines for every hack
  (the default is 64 bytes, see `device-display.md`), so it is the A side of an
  `ab_flash` comparison. `-DPSRAM_BENCH` boots into `diag/psram_bench.h`
  instead of the runner and prints cost per cache miss, sequential rates and a
  working-set sweep; `-DPSRAM_BENCH_VARIANT=0..3` picks the line size and
  prefetch setting.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- The port name changes with the USB socket the board is plugged into
  (`/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` became `/dev/cu.usbmodem101` on 2026-10-14). When
  it is missing, find the board without touching it:
  `ioreg -p IOUSB -l -w0 | grep -E "\+-o|idVendor|idProduct|USB Product
  Name|USB Serial Number"` lists USB devices, and
  `ioreg -r -c IOSerialBSDClient -l | grep IOCalloutDevice` lists the serial
  ports. The StopWatch is the "USB JTAG/serial debug unit" from Espressif
  (`idVendor` 12346, `idProduct` 4097). Its USB serial number is its MAC:
  Rod's board is `28:84:85:43:B2:70`, so check that before flashing a port
  you have not used before. Pass `--upload-port <port>` to `pio run -t upload`

  `upload_port` alone. Still ask Rod before each flash. The auto-mode
  classifier refused a flash to an overridden port once: give Rod the command
  to run with `!`.
- Another session may be using the board. Before flashing, run `lsof
  /dev/cu.usbmodem112401`: a "multiple access on port" upload error was
  another session's serial capture, and esptool's connect resets the board
  under it. Ask Rod before flashing over someone else's run.
- PlatformIO cleans the build directory, image and all, when
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` changes: an `-t nobuild -t upload` with other flags
  finds no `firmware.bin`. To keep several images, give each its own

  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- `heap=` and `psram=` are the reading at the end of a window, not a minimum:
  a hack with a long pause and nothing held in it (Celtic's 5 s `*delay2`)
  reads idle in every window. Sample while it works, or read `rotate ->`.

  grows over a 65 s cycle: mean 15.3, worst window 10.8, and Rod saw an earlier
  build sag under 10 fps before the rotation moved on. Capture a full cycle and

  builds flash them alternately and compare window by window; one reading in
  three captures was an unexplained outlier, so never trust a single pair.

  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.

22	# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas
23	
24	OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
25	`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.
26	
27	- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
28	  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
29	  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
30	  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
31	  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
32	  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
33	- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
34	  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
35	  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
36	  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
37	  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
38	  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
39	  `normals.h` define clashing types.
40	- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
41	  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
42	  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
43	- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
44	  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
45	  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
46	  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
47	- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
48	  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
49	  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
50	  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
51	  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
52	  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
53	- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
54	  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
55	  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
56	  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
57	- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
58	  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
59	  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
60	- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
61	  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
62	- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
63	  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
64	  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
65	- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
66	  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
67	  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
68	  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing: Rubik's wrapper (`rubik_gl.c`) draws its
69	  convex octagon stickers as a triangle fan, and with a polygon offset, since
70	  a sticker is 0.01 above its cube face, about two 16-bit depth steps at the
71	  cube's distance, and the face showed through in patches (7,152 coloured
72	  pixels in the pinned frame, 8,678 with the offset). Unknown Pleasures' rim
73	  loop is drawn too, but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face
74	  (-0.01), so no frame changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting
75	  vertices, and the fifth overwrote the matrices and colours after
76	  `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c` crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now
77	  holds it at the first slot. Check a new hack for both.
78	- A decal drawn a hair above a surface z-fights with it at 16-bit depth, and a
79	  test that only asks whether something drew passes. Count the decal's
80	  coloured pixels, and mutation-check the offset (`test_hacks.c`'s Rubik
81	  sticker test fails at 7,152 without it).
82	- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
83	  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
84	  neither.
85	- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
86	  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
87	  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
88	  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
89	  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
90	  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
91	- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
92	  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
93	  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
94	  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
95	- Unknown Pleasures runs at `*speed: 0.3` (a registry override; the panel dims
96	  after each push by an amount that grows with the scroll per push, see
97	  `device-display.md` and issue #68). The hack halves `*count` at displays of
98	  480 pixels or less, so the default of 80 draws 40 rows and `*count: 40` draws
99	  20. Every new row is added by `tick_unk` (about every 1.2 s at full speed).
100	  Upstream adds it at the end of a draw and restarts its clock at that frame's
101	  time, and the frame was drawn at the scroll's clamp, so the time past the
102	  interval never scrolled: the picture stood still for a push (issue #134,
103	  filmed as a 190 ms stall every seventh push at 40 rows of 50 points).
104	  `unknownpleasures_gl.c` adds the row before the draw and moves the clock on
105	  by one interval. The tick is 12 to 35 ms (software `double` `cos`) and the
106	  TE sync wait absorbs it, so it never stretched a frame. `glLineWidth` is a
107	  no-op in the shim.
108	- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
109	  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
110	  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
111	  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
112	  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
113	  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
114	  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
115	  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
116	  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
117	  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
118	  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
119	  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
120	- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
121	  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
122	  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
123	  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
124	  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
125	  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
126	  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
127	  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
128	  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
129	  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
130	  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
131	  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
132	  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
133	  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
134	- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
135	  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
136	  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
137	  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
138	  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
139	  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
140	  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
141	- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
142	  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
143	  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
144	  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
145	  to reach them.
146	- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
147	  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
148	  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
149	  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
150	  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
151	  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
152	  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
153	  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
154	  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
155	- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
156	  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
157	  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
158	- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
159	  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
160	  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
161	- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
162	  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
163	- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
164	  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
165	  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
166	  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
167	  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
168	  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
169	- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
170	  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
171	  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
172	  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
173	  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
174	  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
175	- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
176	  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
177	  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
178	  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
179	  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
180	- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
181	  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
182	  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
183	  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
184	  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
185	  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
186	  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
187	  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
188	  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
189	  drift from the firmware's rule.
190	- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
191	  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
192	  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
193	  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
194	  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
195	  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
196	  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
197	  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
198	  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
199	  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
200	  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
201	  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
202	  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
203	- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
204	  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
205	- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
206	  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
207	  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
208	  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
209	- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
210	  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
211	  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
212	  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
213	  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
214	  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
215	  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
216	- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
217	  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
218	  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
219	  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
220	  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
221	  the clears that ran, for the tests.
222	- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
223	  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
224	  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
225	  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
226	- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
227	  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
228	  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
229	  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
230	  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
231	  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
232	  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
233	- The push overlap (`repaints_all`, issue #118): before each clear or
234	  primitive, `follow_canvas` points TinyGL's `pbuf` at the current
235	  `canvas->px`. The colour dirty rectangle is kept per buffer (the buffer
236	  just left keeps its box, valid flag and clear colour), so a clear still
237	  rewrites only what was drawn in that buffer; a buffer TinyGL never drew in
238	  gets a full clear. The box last drawn in the buffer just left is marked
239	  erased, since that is what the display shows. The swap does not follow:
240	  a frame that draws nothing must mark nothing, or the push would send the
241	  older frame the new buffer holds. If the two buffers' clear colours
242	  differ, the switch marks the whole canvas: the clear finds its own buffer
243	  already that colour and rewrites nothing (red, green, red left the
244	  display green). `glshim_canvas_overwritten()` forces a full clear for
245	  writers other than TinyGL (`test_push_overlap`'s noise
246	  run). Not for a scale-2 hack (`double_into_canvas` writes only the box) or
247	  Pipes (skips clears). Pinned A/B, plain to overlapped: Bubble3D 11.2 to
248	  12.0 fps, Gears 15.2 to 16.5, CubicGrid 15.3 to 19.5, StonerView 36.4 to
249	  43.8, HexTrail 15.2 to 20.5 before its first restart; Morph3D about 3%
250	  (small push), unflagged. The step grew 5 to 10 ms with both cores on
251	  PSRAM.
252	- The swap marks two bounding boxes (erased, drawn), not a list of
253	  regions: a drawing in the top half and an erase in the bottom one mark
254	  every row between. A test that asserts a row stays clean must keep both
255	  frames' drawings on one side of it (`corner_frame(f % 2)`).
256	- Board profiles (issue #43): `-DGL_PROFILE` prints a `glprof` line after
257	  each `run` line with cycle counts per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
258	  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill), and
259	  `tools/ab_flash.py` builds variants pinned, flashes them in turn and
260	  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:
261	  PlatformIO cleans a build directory, image and all, when the build flags
262	  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
263	  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.
264	- Lazy lighting is the default (`GL_LAZY_SHADE`; `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` restores
265	  TinyGL's order): a vertex is lit when something that uses it is drawn, so
266	  culled triangles cost nothing. Gears 61.1 to 57.7 ms, Morph3D 61.4 to
267	  58.4 ms, frame hashes unchanged. `GL_IRAM` (still a switch) and two
268	  experiments since removed, matrix stacks in internal RAM and the data
269	  cache's next-line prefetch (autoload) over PSRAM, moved Gears by under 1 ms.
270	  The prefetch needs a region that holds only mapped pages: over the whole
271	  32 MB data bus it boot-looped the board (the panic handler faulted too), and
272	  a region worked out from an allocation's address cannot promise that.
273	- Fill is compute-bound, not PSRAM-miss-bound. A new PSRAM cache line costs
274	  129 cycles to read and about 220 to read and write back (the `membench`
275	  line of a profile build), but neighbouring triangles reuse lines. A banded
276	  renderer that held a frame's triangles and replayed them into 32-row bands
277	  in internal RAM was exact but slower: Gears 59 to 76 ms (replay 38 ms
278	  against 30 ms of direct fill), Hypnowheel 476 to 528 ms. It was reverted
279	  (`feature/43-banded-renderer` history). Faster fill needs fewer cycles a
280	  pixel or fewer pixels, not other memory.
281	- Every `Replace` anchor in `tinygl_patch.py` must be upstream text: the
282	  anchor tests delete it from the unpatched source. To add next to text an
283	  earlier patch inserted, extend that patch's replacement instead.
284	- Resolving a merge conflict in `tools/tinygl_patch.py`: the conflict region
285	  can span the ends of `REPLACEMENTS`, `LATE_REPLACEMENTS` and `HOT_FUNCTIONS`,
286	  so keeping both sides can put an entry in the wrong tuple (a `Replace` among
287	  the `Hot` entries fails collection with "'Replace' object has no attribute
288	  'definition'"). Check each kept entry's tuple. `ruff format` on the file also
289	  rewraps an `AA_LINE +` line nobody touched; revert that hunk.
290	- `glshim_set_render_scale(2)`, read by the next `glshim_open`, renders at half
291	  the width and height: `glViewport` is a macro for `glshim_Viewport`, which
292	  divides by the scale, and the swap doubles the dirty box into the canvas.
293	  Hypnowheel's fill went from 334 to 129 ms (not a quarter: rows and triangles
294	  still cost). Nothing registered uses it.
295	- Added for the 2026-10-12 batch, each test-first: `glInterleavedArrays` for
296	  `GL_V3F`, `GL_C3F_V3F` and `GL_N3F_V3F` (what `gllist.c` uses);
297	  `glTexImage2D` converting RGBA and luminance bytes to RGB (TinyGL exits on
298	  anything but three-component `GL_RGB`); `glColor4ub`; `glTexGeni`,
299	  `glDepthFunc` and `glTexEnvf` accepted and ignored; `glTexParameterf`; the
300	  OpenGL 1.2 colour-control names; and `texfont.h` (`texfont.c`), which draws
301	  TinyGL's public-domain 8x8 font as quads at half the point size.
302	- TinyGL fills a quad over [10, 16] by [23, 24] as columns 9 to 15 and both
303	  rows: its edges are inclusive, so test text and thin quads by their box,
304	  not a pixel count. Its lit textures can lose a step of a channel.
305	- TinyGL prints a warning for every `glEnable` it does not know, each time,
306	  which on the board goes to the serial log every frame: filter them in the
307	  wrapper.
308	- Pipes (issue #44, `hacks/pipes_gl.c`) skips work no other GL hack can: with
309	  its camera fixed (`*rotatepipes: False`), when the clear, both matrices and
310	  the lists called so far match last frame, it skips the clear and those lists
311	  and draws only the new piece. Two traps, each caught by
312	  `test_pipes_incremental_redraw_matches_a_full_redraw`: a new screen
313	  recompiles the same list names, so any `glNewList` must end the skipping; and
314	  the next screen must be generated at the start of a draw, as upstream's fade
315	  does, because `generate_system` clears, and a clear after the swap erased the
316	  frame just shown in a full redraw. `pipes_full_redraw` turns the skipping off
317	  for the tests.
318	- Pipes compiles every display list of a screen when the screen starts, and a
319	  list holds each vertex expanded (a 16 by 16 sphere from `glDrawArrays` is
320	  about 17 KB). Board PSRAM sets the screen size (`-DPIPES_CYCLES`,
321	  `-DPIPES_SIZE`), and TinyGL does not check a list's allocation, so running
322	  out crashes: 3 systems of 150 left 1.9 MB free. Host heap for the same lists
323	  is about twice the board's (8-byte list words).
324	- Pipes' helpers: `teapot.c` is built with `HAVE_JWZGLES` (a triangle table,
325	  `teapot2.h`, instead of evaluators TinyGL lacks). That table was 228 KB of
326	  flash; since #104 `firmware/teapot_table.py` writes `generated/teapot/`, a
327	  byte-identical copy of `teapot.c` beside a `teapot2.h` holding the floats
328	  deflated (37 KB), so the copy's quoted include finds ours first.
329	  `glshim/glx_teapot.c` renames upstream's `unit_teapot` and unpacks the table
330	  into 227 KB of PSRAM only while it runs (Pipes calls it once, compiling a
331	  list); with no memory the teapot is an empty list. `test_glshim` compares
332	  the unpacked floats with upstream's. `buildlwo.c` maps `GL_POLYGON` to
333	  `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN` in its own wrapper only (issue #80 is the general
334	  question).

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing: Rubik's wrapper (`rubik_gl.c`) draws its
  convex octagon stickers as a triangle fan, and with a polygon offset, since
  a sticker is 0.01 above its cube face, about two 16-bit depth steps at the
  cube's distance, and the face showed through in patches (7,152 coloured
  pixels in the pinned frame, 8,678 with the offset). Unknown Pleasures' rim
  loop is drawn too, but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face
  (-0.01), so no frame changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting
  vertices, and the fifth overwrote the matrices and colours after
  `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c` crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now
  holds it at the first slot. Check a new hack for both.
- A decal drawn a hair above a surface z-fights with it at 16-bit depth, and a
  test that only asks whether something drew passes. Count the decal's
  coloured pixels, and mutation-check the offset (`test_hacks.c`'s Rubik
  sticker test fails at 7,152 without it).
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- Unknown Pleasures runs at `*speed: 0.3` (a registry override; the panel dims
  after each push by an amount that grows with the scroll per push, see
  `device-display.md` and issue #68). The hack halves `*count` at displays of
  480 pixels or less, so the default of 80 draws 40 rows and `*count: 40` draws
  20. Every new row is added by `tick_unk` (about every 1.2 s at full speed).
  Upstream adds it at the end of a draw and restarts its clock at that frame's
  time, and the frame was drawn at the scroll's clamp, so the time past the
  interval never scrolled: the picture stood still for a push (issue #134,
  filmed as a 190 ms stall every seventh push at 40 rows of 50 points).
  `unknownpleasures_gl.c` adds the row before the draw and moves the clock on
  by one interval. The tick is 12 to 35 ms (software `double` `cos`) and the
  TE sync wait absorbs it, so it never stretched a frame. `glLineWidth` is a
  no-op in the shim.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
  to reach them.
- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
  drift from the firmware's rule.
- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
  the clears that ran, for the tests.
- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
- The push overlap (`repaints_all`, issue #118): before each clear or
  primitive, `follow_canvas` points TinyGL's `pbuf` at the current
  `canvas->px`. The colour dirty rectangle is kept per buffer (the buffer
  just left keeps its box, valid flag and clear colour), so a clear still
  rewrites only what was drawn in that buffer; a buffer TinyGL never drew in
  gets a full clear. The box last drawn in the buffer just left is marked
  erased, since that is what the display shows. The swap does not follow:
  a frame that draws nothing must mark nothing, or the push would send the
  older frame the new buffer holds. If the two buffers' clear colours
  differ, the switch marks the whole canvas: the clear finds its own buffer
  already that colour and rewrites nothing (red, green, red left the
  display green). `glshim_canvas_overwritten()` forces a full clear for
  writers other than TinyGL (`test_push_overlap`'s noise
  run). Not for a scale-2 hack (`double_into_canvas` writes only the box) or
  Pipes (skips clears). Pinned A/B, plain to overlapped: Bubble3D 11.2 to
  12.0 fps, Gears 15.2 to 16.5, CubicGrid 15.3 to 19.5, StonerView 36.4 to
  43.8, HexTrail 15.2 to 20.5 before its first restart; Morph3D about 3%
  (small push), unflagged. The step grew 5 to 10 ms with both cores on
  PSRAM.
- The swap marks two bounding boxes (erased, drawn), not a list of
  regions: a drawing in the top half and an erase in the bottom one mark
  every row between. A test that asserts a row stays clean must keep both
  frames' drawings on one side of it (`corner_frame(f % 2)`).
- Board profiles (issue #43): `-DGL_PROFILE` prints a `glprof` line after
  each `run` line with cycle counts per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill), and
  `tools/ab_flash.py` builds variants pinned, flashes them in turn and
  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:
  PlatformIO cleans a build directory, image and all, when the build flags
  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.
- Lazy lighting is the default (`GL_LAZY_SHADE`; `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` restores
  TinyGL's order): a vertex is lit when something that uses it is drawn, so
  culled triangles cost nothing. Gears 61.1 to 57.7 ms, Morph3D 61.4 to
  58.4 ms, frame hashes unchanged. `GL_IRAM` (still a switch) and two
  experiments since removed, matrix stacks in internal RAM and the data
  cache's next-line prefetch (autoload) over PSRAM, moved Gears by under 1 ms.
  The prefetch needs a region that holds only mapped pages: over the whole
  32 MB data bus it boot-looped the board (the panic handler faulted too), and
  a region worked out from an allocation's address cannot promise that.
- Fill is compute-bound, not PSRAM-miss-bound. A new PSRAM cache line costs
  129 cycles to read and about 220 to read and write back (the `membench`
  line of a profile build), but neighbouring triangles reuse lines. A banded
  renderer that held a frame's triangles and replayed them into 32-row bands
  in internal RAM was exact but slower: Gears 59 to 76 ms (replay 38 ms
  against 30 ms of direct fill), Hypnowheel 476 to 528 ms. It was reverted
  (`feature/43-banded-renderer` history). Faster fill needs fewer cycles a
  pixel or fewer pixels, not other memory.
- Every `Replace` anchor in `tinygl_patch.py` must be upstream text: the
  anchor tests delete it from the unpatched source. To add next to text an
  earlier patch inserted, extend that patch's replacement instead.
- Resolving a merge conflict in `tools/tinygl_patch.py`: the conflict region
  can span the ends of `REPLACEMENTS`, `LATE_REPLACEMENTS` and `HOT_FUNCTIONS`,
  so keeping both sides can put an entry in the wrong tuple (a `Replace` among
  the `Hot` entries fails collection with "'Replace' object has no attribute
  'definition'"). Check each kept entry's tuple. `ruff format` on the file also
  rewraps an `AA_LINE +` line nobody touched; revert that hunk.
- `glshim_set_render_scale(2)`, read by the next `glshim_open`, renders at half
  the width and height: `glViewport` is a macro for `glshim_Viewport`, which
  divides by the scale, and the swap doubles the dirty box into the canvas.
  Hypnowheel's fill went from 334 to 129 ms (not a quarter: rows and triangles
  still cost). Nothing registered uses it.
- Added for the 2026-10-12 batch, each test-first: `glInterleavedArrays` for
  `GL_V3F`, `GL_C3F_V3F` and `GL_N3F_V3F` (what `gllist.c` uses);
  `glTexImage2D` converting RGBA and luminance bytes to RGB (TinyGL exits on
  anything but three-component `GL_RGB`); `glColor4ub`; `glTexGeni`,
  `glDepthFunc` and `glTexEnvf` accepted and ignored; `glTexParameterf`; the
  OpenGL 1.2 colour-control names; and `texfont.h` (`texfont.c`), which draws
  TinyGL's public-domain 8x8 font as quads at half the point size.
- TinyGL fills a quad over [10, 16] by [23, 24] as columns 9 to 15 and both
  rows: its edges are inclusive, so test text and thin quads by their box,
  not a pixel count. Its lit textures can lose a step of a channel.
- TinyGL prints a warning for every `glEnable` it does not know, each time,
  which on the board goes to the serial log every frame: filter them in the
  wrapper.
- Pipes (issue #44, `hacks/pipes_gl.c`) skips work no other GL hack can: with
  its camera fixed (`*rotatepipes: False`), when the clear, both matrices and
  the lists called so far match last frame, it skips the clear and those lists
  and draws only the new piece. Two traps, each caught by
  `test_pipes_incremental_redraw_matches_a_full_redraw`: a new screen
  recompiles the same list names, so any `glNewList` must end the skipping; and
  the next screen must be generated at the start of a draw, as upstream's fade
  does, because `generate_system` clears, and a clear after the swap erased the
  frame just shown in a full redraw. `pipes_full_redraw` turns the skipping off
  for the tests.
- Pipes compiles every display list of a screen when the screen starts, and a
  list holds each vertex expanded (a 16 by 16 sphere from `glDrawArrays` is
  about 17 KB). Board PSRAM sets the screen size (`-DPIPES_CYCLES`,
  `-DPIPES_SIZE`), and TinyGL does not check a list's allocation, so running
  out crashes: 3 systems of 150 left 1.9 MB free. Host heap for the same lists
  is about twice the board's (8-byte list words).
- Pipes' helpers: `teapot.c` is built with `HAVE_JWZGLES` (a triangle table,
  `teapot2.h`, instead of evaluators TinyGL lacks). That table was 228 KB of
  flash; since #104 `firmware/teapot_table.py` writes `generated/teapot/`, a
  byte-identical copy of `teapot.c` beside a `teapot2.h` holding the floats
  deflated (37 KB), so the copy's quoted include finds ours first.
  `glshim/glx_teapot.c` renames upstream's `unit_teapot` and unpacks the table
  into 227 KB of PSRAM only while it runs (Pipes calls it once, compiling a
  list); with no memory the teapot is an empty list. `test_glshim` compares
  the unpacked floats with upstream's. `buildlwo.c` maps `GL_POLYGON` to
  `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN` in its own wrapper only (issue #80 is the general
  question).

# Porting a batch of hacks

For several hacks on one branch, with Rod away. The per-hack steps are in
`SKILL.md` and `adding-a-hack.md`; this is what a batch adds. Per-hack findings
live in `.claude/rules/hacks.md`, not here.

## Order of work

1. Read every header before copying anything: a `(GPL)` tag or an xlock notice
   changes the notices row, and a licence that is not a permission notice means
   stop and ask.
2. Triage by gap count. Do the easy ones first: they pay for shim gaps the
   others need. Leave GL and anything under a few fps to last.
3. One branch, a commit per hack, shim code test-first and mutation-checked.
   No PR until Rod says.
4. `uv run tools/wire_hack.py <name> <Class> "<copyright>"` copies the file and
   registers it with a frame hash of `0` (skipped), so every commit stays green.
   Then `pio run -e dump`, fill the gaps, dump frames at several counts and
   look at them.
5. Flash and measure each hack as soon as it runs
   (`bash tools/flash_and_capture.sh <hack> 30`). Report measured, unjudged and
   unseen separately.
6. Pin all the new hashes in one run, after looking at the frames:
   `HACK_PINS_OUT=<file> pio test -e native -f test_hacks`.
7. Soak the whole registry before handing over: `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` for five
   laps, then look for a reboot, a panic or a "Stack canary", and compare PSRAM
   on each visit of the new hacks (it should match exactly).
8. Measured rows, rules, a regenerated assessment, and a notes file for Rod: what
   to look at, which choices are his, what was not measured. His review changes
   the numbers (a hack dropped, one retuned), so rewrite the notes after it or
   put the final state in the PR body, which is the record. A stale notes file
   misleads.

## Traps

| Trap | Do |
| --- | --- |
| A change that is not pixel-identical by construction (single precision, a faster fill) and you only checked fps | Look at a frame. A hack drew garbage for hours at "20 fps" |
| `#define double float` before a header that has `double` in a struct a shim `.c` shares | Include that header first, then the define; a flat-screen test guards it |
| A hack that keeps state in statics across starts | Its pin depends on earlier tests; reset the static in a wrapper, and test both outcomes |
| A mode picked with `random()` | A boot is deterministic, so measure the other mode by forcing it |
| Constants in pixels or frames, tuned for another window size or frame rate | Scale them at build time (`tools/fireworkx_patch.py`), not by editing the copy |
| A hack that treats `malloc(0) == NULL` as out of memory | The board returns NULL for zero bytes, the host a pointer: it stops drawing on the board only. Reproduce with an allocator hook that fails for zero |
| A stop that leaks | `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0 out.raw` names the line (rebuild `-e dump` first) |

## Finding the cost

Skip one thing behind a temporary flag and read `step=`; revert it. Guessing
was wrong three times running. The usual causes here:

- full-frame passes over PSRAM: a clear, a copy, a blur, a 565 conversion (render
  smaller, alias a pixmap to the window, erase only what was drawn)
- the shim's polygon fill, which divides in double (`hacks/float_polygon.h`)
- soft double: `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm <object> | grep ' U __.*df'`; `frand` hides
  a `1.0` in its macro body (`hacks/single_frand.h`)
- a pause the hack asks for (`wait=`): override `*delay` and say the pace changed
- a GL hack's clear and push, which scale with the dirty box, and work the GL
  layer does that nothing reads (a depth clear with the depth test off):
  `gl_budget.py` shows vertices submitted against triangles drawn

## Choices for Rod

When look and speed trade off, leave a build flag per option, measure each, and
register the one nearer his bar. After his hands-on notes, expect to retune or
drop: from seven ports he kept six and dropped Boing, and asked for HexTrail to
be faster. Keep a flashable rotation build ready (`-DROTATE_SECONDS=25`, the new
hacks first) and say which build the board holds when you stop.

## Tools

| --- | --- |
| Register a hack | `tools/wire_hack.py` |
| Flash a pinned build and read the serial log | `tools/flash_and_capture.sh`, `tools/serial_capture.py` |
| Does a test notice a break | `tools/mutate.py <file> 'old=>new' --cmd '...'` |
| Pin hashes | `HACK_PINS_OUT` (above) |

# Adding a hack

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md. The order of work is in `SKILL.md`.

The `port-hack` skill orders this work, says what to read for before copying a
hack, and holds a recipe per trap. The steps:

1. Check its row in `docs/porting-assessment.md` (effort and Speed band) and
   read its licence header.
2. Update the expected list in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` and see
   it fail. Add `test_<name>_stops_do_not_leak` beside the others, and
   mutation-check it: remove each free a wrapper adds and watch it fail.
3. Copy the file to `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/<name>.c`, add the notices row
   and an `extern` plus entry in `hacks/registry.c`.
4. Fill shim gaps test-first in `firmware/test/test_xshim/`. The compile
   check in `score_hacks.py` shows what is missing.
5. Host tests pass, dump a frame and look at it, then (with Rod's go-ahead)
   flash and measure fps and free heap/PSRAM over serial. To pin its frame
   hash after looking at the frame, put `0x1ull` in `kBaseline`, run
   `pio test -e native -f test_hacks`, convert the "Was N" in the failure line
   with `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"`, and run it again. A new hack never gets
   `0` in `kBaseline`: `0` is for a hack left unpinned on purpose, with the
   reason in its comment (DecayScreen, RotZoomer).
6. Regenerate the assessment and add measurements to
   `tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, then re-run the speed backtest: each port
   adds a point to the check of the Speed bands, which were fitted to the first
   29 hacks. To make a port a real test, commit its host time and predicted
   range first (`docs/speed-predictions.md` shows the form), flash it as copied,
   and add its name to `HOLDOUT` in `tools/speed_backtest.py`. The first four
   (Mountain, Epicycle, Kaleidescope, Celtic) all fell where predicted.
7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (for a
   plain screenhack, `hacks/substrate_single.c`; the recipe is in the skill's
   `techniques.md`), and compare double and float frames at several frame
   counts. A resource
   override can skip a hack's restart cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so
   leak-test any override.
8. If Rod drops a port after seeing it (Hypnowheel, Boing; Celtic was dropped
   and came back through issue #37): remove it
   from `g_hacks[]`, the expected list, its hash and its leak test; keep the
   source and notices row; add `name: reason` (short: it is printed as a
   bullet) to `tools/failed_ports.txt`. For a GL hack, keep the `<name>_gl.c`
   wrapper but exclude it and the directory (`-<hacks/boing/>
   -<hacks/boing_gl.c>`) in all three `build_src_filter` lines, or it still
   builds. A reason Rod gave in his own words ("boring on a small screen") is
   the reason to record. File an issue only if there is something to come back
   to.
   Unhook its build steps too: its entry in `patch_float_literals.py` and any
   pre-script only it needs (BlockTube's `gl_textures.py`), or every build
   still runs them and fails without their `vendor/` input.
9. A header that a pre-script writes into the build dir (the font, the grab
   image) must be included under `__has_include` in `native/dump_main.c`:
   `tools/probe_hacks.py` compiles that file without the build's generated
   directory, and an unconditional include failed two `test_probe_hacks`
   cases. Add the pre-script to all three `extra_scripts` lines in
   `platformio.ini`, and a wrapper's original source to all three
   `build_src_filter` lines (`sed -i.bak 's|<last entry>$|<last entry> <new>|'`
   does all three).
