22	# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas
23	
24	OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
25	`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.
26	
27	- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
28	  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
29	  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
30	  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
31	  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
32	  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
33	- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
34	  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
35	  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
36	  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
37	  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
38	  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
39	  `normals.h` define clashing types.
40	- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
41	  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
42	  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
43	- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
44	  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
45	  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
46	  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
47	- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
48	  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
49	  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
50	  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
51	  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
52	  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
53	- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
54	  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
55	  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
56	  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
57	- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
58	  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
59	  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
60	- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
61	  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
62	- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
63	  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
64	  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
65	- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
66	  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
67	  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
68	  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing: Rubik's wrapper (`rubik_gl.c`) draws its
69	  convex octagon stickers as a triangle fan, and with a polygon offset, since
70	  a sticker is 0.01 above its cube face, about two 16-bit depth steps at the
71	  cube's distance, and the face showed through in patches (7,152 coloured
72	  pixels in the pinned frame, 8,678 with the offset). Unknown Pleasures' rim
73	  loop is drawn too, but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face
74	  (-0.01), so no frame changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting
75	  vertices, and the fifth overwrote the matrices and colours after
76	  `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c` crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now
77	  holds it at the first slot. Check a new hack for both.
78	- A decal drawn a hair above a surface z-fights with it at 16-bit depth, and a
79	  test that only asks whether something drew passes. Count the decal's
80	  coloured pixels, and mutation-check the offset (`test_hacks.c`'s Rubik
81	  sticker test fails at 7,152 without it).
82	- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
83	  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
84	  neither.
85	- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
86	  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
87	  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
88	  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
89	  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
90	  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
91	- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
92	  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
93	  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
94	  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
95	- Unknown Pleasures runs at `*speed: 0.3` (a registry override; the panel dims
96	  after each push by an amount that grows with the scroll per push, see
97	  `device-display.md` and issue #68). The hack halves `*count` at displays of
98	  480 pixels or less, so the default of 80 draws 40 rows and `*count: 40` draws
99	  20. Every new row is added by `tick_unk` (about every 1.2 s at full speed).
100	  Upstream adds it at the end of a draw and restarts its clock at that frame's
101	  time, and the frame was drawn at the scroll's clamp, so the time past the
102	  interval never scrolled: the picture stood still for a push (issue #134,
103	  filmed as a 190 ms stall every seventh push at 40 rows of 50 points).
104	  `unknownpleasures_gl.c` adds the row before the draw and moves the clock on
105	  by one interval. The tick is 12 to 35 ms (software `double` `cos`) and the
106	  TE sync wait absorbs it, so it never stretched a frame. `glLineWidth` is a
107	  no-op in the shim.
108	- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
109	  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
110	  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
111	  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
112	  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
113	  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
114	  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
115	  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
116	  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
117	  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
118	  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
119	  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
120	- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
121	  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
122	  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
123	  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
124	  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
125	  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
126	  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
127	  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
128	  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
129	  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
130	  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
131	  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
132	  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
133	  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
134	- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
135	  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
136	  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
137	  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
138	  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
139	  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
140	  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
141	- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
142	  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
143	  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
144	  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
145	  to reach them.
146	- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
147	  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
148	  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
149	  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
150	  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
151	  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
152	  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
153	  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
154	  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
155	- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
156	  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
157	  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
158	- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
159	  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
160	  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
161	- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
162	  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
163	- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
164	  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
165	  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
166	  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
167	  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
168	  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
169	- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
170	  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
171	  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
172	  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
173	  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
174	  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
175	- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
176	  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
177	  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
178	  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
179	  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
180	- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
181	  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
182	  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
183	  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
184	  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
185	  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
186	  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
187	  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
188	  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
189	  drift from the firmware's rule.
190	- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
191	  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
192	  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
193	  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
194	  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
195	  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
196	  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
197	  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
198	  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
199	  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
200	  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
201	  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
202	  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
203	- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
204	  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
205	- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
206	  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
207	  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
208	  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
209	- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
210	  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
211	  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
212	  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
213	  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
214	  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
215	  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
216	- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
217	  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
218	  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
219	  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
220	  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
221	  the clears that ran, for the tests.
222	- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
223	  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
224	  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
225	  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
226	- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
227	  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
228	  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
229	  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
230	  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
231	  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
232	  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
233	- The push overlap (`repaints_all`, issue #118): before each clear or
234	  primitive, `follow_canvas` points TinyGL's `pbuf` at the current
235	  `canvas->px`. The colour dirty rectangle is kept per buffer (the buffer
236	  just left keeps its box, valid flag and clear colour), so a clear still
237	  rewrites only what was drawn in that buffer; a buffer TinyGL never drew in
238	  gets a full clear. The box last drawn in the buffer just left is marked
239	  erased, since that is what the display shows. The swap does not follow:
240	  a frame that draws nothing must mark nothing, or the push would send the
241	  older frame the new buffer holds. If the two buffers' clear colours
242	  differ, the switch marks the whole canvas: the clear finds its own buffer
243	  already that colour and rewrites nothing (red, green, red left the
244	  display green). `glshim_canvas_overwritten()` forces a full clear for
245	  writers other than TinyGL (`test_push_overlap`'s noise
246	  run). Not for a scale-2 hack (`double_into_canvas` writes only the box) or
247	  Pipes (skips clears). Pinned A/B, plain to overlapped: Bubble3D 11.2 to
248	  12.0 fps, Gears 15.2 to 16.5, CubicGrid 15.3 to 19.5, StonerView 36.4 to
249	  43.8, HexTrail 15.2 to 20.5 before its first restart; Morph3D about 3%
250	  (small push), unflagged. The step grew 5 to 10 ms with both cores on
251	  PSRAM.
252	- The swap marks two bounding boxes (erased, drawn), not a list of
253	  regions: a drawing in the top half and an erase in the bottom one mark
254	  every row between. A test that asserts a row stays clean must keep both
255	  frames' drawings on one side of it (`corner_frame(f % 2)`).
256	- Board profiles (issue #43): `-DGL_PROFILE` prints a `glprof` line after
257	  each `run` line with cycle counts per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
258	  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill), and
259	  `tools/ab_flash.py` builds variants pinned, flashes them in turn and
260	  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:
261	  PlatformIO cleans a build directory, image and all, when the build flags
262	  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
263	  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.
264	- Lazy lighting is the default (`GL_LAZY_SHADE`; `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` restores
265	  TinyGL's order): a vertex is lit when something that uses it is drawn, so
266	  culled triangles cost nothing. Gears 61.1 to 57.7 ms, Morph3D 61.4 to
267	  58.4 ms, frame hashes unchanged. `GL_IRAM` (still a switch) and two
268	  experiments since removed, matrix stacks in internal RAM and the data
269	  cache's next-line prefetch (autoload) over PSRAM, moved Gears by under 1 ms.
270	  The prefetch needs a region that holds only mapped pages: over the whole
271	  32 MB data bus it boot-looped the board (the panic handler faulted too), and
272	  a region worked out from an allocation's address cannot promise that.
273	- Fill is compute-bound, not PSRAM-miss-bound. A new PSRAM cache line costs
274	  129 cycles to read and about 220 to read and write back (the `membench`
275	  line of a profile build), but neighbouring triangles reuse lines. A banded
276	  renderer that held a frame's triangles and replayed them into 32-row bands
277	  in internal RAM was exact but slower: Gears 59 to 76 ms (replay 38 ms
278	  against 30 ms of direct fill), Hypnowheel 476 to 528 ms. It was reverted
279	  (`feature/43-banded-renderer` history). Faster fill needs fewer cycles a
280	  pixel or fewer pixels, not other memory.
281	- Every `Replace` anchor in `tinygl_patch.py` must be upstream text: the
282	  anchor tests delete it from the unpatched source. To add next to text an
283	  earlier patch inserted, extend that patch's replacement instead.
284	- Resolving a merge conflict in `tools/tinygl_patch.py`: the conflict region
285	  can span the ends of `REPLACEMENTS`, `LATE_REPLACEMENTS` and `HOT_FUNCTIONS`,
286	  so keeping both sides can put an entry in the wrong tuple (a `Replace` among
287	  the `Hot` entries fails collection with "'Replace' object has no attribute
288	  'definition'"). Check each kept entry's tuple. `ruff format` on the file also
289	  rewraps an `AA_LINE +` line nobody touched; revert that hunk.
290	- `glshim_set_render_scale(2)`, read by the next `glshim_open`, renders at half
291	  the width and height: `glViewport` is a macro for `glshim_Viewport`, which
292	  divides by the scale, and the swap doubles the dirty box into the canvas.
293	  Hypnowheel's fill went from 334 to 129 ms (not a quarter: rows and triangles
294	  still cost). Nothing registered uses it.
295	- Added for the 2026-10-12 batch, each test-first: `glInterleavedArrays` for
296	  `GL_V3F`, `GL_C3F_V3F` and `GL_N3F_V3F` (what `gllist.c` uses);
297	  `glTexImage2D` converting RGBA and luminance bytes to RGB (TinyGL exits on
298	  anything but three-component `GL_RGB`); `glColor4ub`; `glTexGeni`,
299	  `glDepthFunc` and `glTexEnvf` accepted and ignored; `glTexParameterf`; the
300	  OpenGL 1.2 colour-control names; and `texfont.h` (`texfont.c`), which draws
301	  TinyGL's public-domain 8x8 font as quads at half the point size.
302	- TinyGL fills a quad over [10, 16] by [23, 24] as columns 9 to 15 and both
303	  rows: its edges are inclusive, so test text and thin quads by their box,
304	  not a pixel count. Its lit textures can lose a step of a channel.
305	- TinyGL prints a warning for every `glEnable` it does not know, each time,
306	  which on the board goes to the serial log every frame: filter them in the
307	  wrapper.
308	- Pipes (issue #44, `hacks/pipes_gl.c`) skips work no other GL hack can: with
309	  its camera fixed (`*rotatepipes: False`), when the clear, both matrices and
310	  the lists called so far match last frame, it skips the clear and those lists
311	  and draws only the new piece. Two traps, each caught by
312	  `test_pipes_incremental_redraw_matches_a_full_redraw`: a new screen
313	  recompiles the same list names, so any `glNewList` must end the skipping; and
314	  the next screen must be generated at the start of a draw, as upstream's fade
315	  does, because `generate_system` clears, and a clear after the swap erased the
316	  frame just shown in a full redraw. `pipes_full_redraw` turns the skipping off
317	  for the tests.
318	- Pipes compiles every display list of a screen when the screen starts, and a
319	  list holds each vertex expanded (a 16 by 16 sphere from `glDrawArrays` is
320	  about 17 KB). Board PSRAM sets the screen size (`-DPIPES_CYCLES`,
321	  `-DPIPES_SIZE`), and TinyGL does not check a list's allocation, so running
322	  out crashes: 3 systems of 150 left 1.9 MB free. Host heap for the same lists
323	  is about twice the board's (8-byte list words).
324	- Pipes' helpers: `teapot.c` is built with `HAVE_JWZGLES` (a triangle table,
325	  `teapot2.h`, instead of evaluators TinyGL lacks). That table was 228 KB of
326	  flash; since #104 `firmware/teapot_table.py` writes `generated/teapot/`, a
327	  byte-identical copy of `teapot.c` beside a `teapot2.h` holding the floats
328	  deflated (37 KB), so the copy's quoted include finds ours first.
329	  `glshim/glx_teapot.c` renames upstream's `unit_teapot` and unpacks the table
330	  into 227 KB of PSRAM only while it runs (Pipes calls it once, compiling a
331	  list); with no memory the teapot is an empty list. `test_glshim` compares
332	  the unpacked floats with upstream's. `buildlwo.c` maps `GL_POLYGON` to
333	  `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN` in its own wrapper only (issue #80 is the general
334	  question).

1	# Porting a batch of hacks
2	
3	For several hacks on one branch, with Rod away. The per-hack steps are in
4	`SKILL.md` and `adding-a-hack.md`; this is what a batch adds. Per-hack findings
5	live in `.claude/rules/hacks.md`, not here.
6	
7	## Order of work
8	
9	1. Read every header before copying anything: a `(GPL)` tag or an xlock notice
10	   changes the notices row, and a licence that is not a permission notice means
11	   stop and ask.
12	2. Triage by gap count. Do the easy ones first: they pay for shim gaps the
13	   others need. Leave GL and anything under a few fps to last.
14	3. One branch, a commit per hack, shim code test-first and mutation-checked.
15	   No PR until Rod says.
16	4. `uv run tools/wire_hack.py <name> <Class> "<copyright>"` copies the file and
17	   registers it with a frame hash of `0` (skipped), so every commit stays green.
18	   Then `pio run -e dump`, fill the gaps, dump frames at several counts and
19	   look at them.
20	5. Flash and measure each hack as soon as it runs
21	   (`bash tools/flash_and_capture.sh <hack> 30`). Report measured, unjudged and
22	   unseen separately.
23	6. Pin all the new hashes in one run, after looking at the frames:
24	   `HACK_PINS_OUT=<file> pio test -e native -f test_hacks`.
25	7. Soak the whole registry before handing over: `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` for five
26	   laps, then look for a reboot, a panic or a "Stack canary", and compare PSRAM
27	   on each visit of the new hacks (it should match exactly).
28	8. Measured rows, rules, a regenerated assessment, and a notes file for Rod: what
29	   to look at, which choices are his, what was not measured. His review changes
30	   the numbers (a hack dropped, one retuned), so rewrite the notes after it or
31	   put the final state in the PR body, which is the record. A stale notes file
32	   misleads.
33	
34	## Traps
35	
36	| Trap | Do |
37	| --- | --- |
38	| A change that is not pixel-identical by construction (single precision, a faster fill) and you only checked fps | Look at a frame. A hack drew garbage for hours at "20 fps" |
39	| `#define double float` before a header that has `double` in a struct a shim `.c` shares | Include that header first, then the define; a flat-screen test guards it |
40	| A hack that keeps state in statics across starts | Its pin depends on earlier tests; reset the static in a wrapper, and test both outcomes |
41	| A mode picked with `random()` | A boot is deterministic, so measure the other mode by forcing it |
42	| Constants in pixels or frames, tuned for another window size or frame rate | Scale them at build time (`tools/fireworkx_patch.py`), not by editing the copy |
43	| A hack that treats `malloc(0) == NULL` as out of memory | The board returns NULL for zero bytes, the host a pointer: it stops drawing on the board only. Reproduce with an allocator hook that fails for zero |
44	| A stop that leaks | `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0 out.raw` names the line (rebuild `-e dump` first) |
45	
46	## Finding the cost
47	
48	Skip one thing behind a temporary flag and read `step=`; revert it. Guessing
49	was wrong three times running. The usual causes here:
50	
51	- full-frame passes over PSRAM: a clear, a copy, a blur, a 565 conversion (render
52	  smaller, alias a pixmap to the window, erase only what was drawn)
53	- the shim's polygon fill, which divides in double (`hacks/float_polygon.h`)
54	- soft double: `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm <object> | grep ' U __.*df'`; `frand` hides
55	  a `1.0` in its macro body (`hacks/single_frand.h`)
56	- a pause the hack asks for (`wait=`): override `*delay` and say the pace changed
57	- a GL hack's clear and push, which scale with the dirty box, and work the GL
58	  layer does that nothing reads (a depth clear with the depth test off):
59	  `gl_budget.py` shows vertices submitted against triangles drawn
60	
61	## Choices for Rod
62	
63	When look and speed trade off, leave a build flag per option, measure each, and
64	register the one nearer his bar. After his hands-on notes, expect to retune or
65	drop: from seven ports he kept six and dropped Boing, and asked for HexTrail to
66	be faster. Keep a flashable rotation build ready (`-DROTATE_SECONDS=25`, the new
67	hacks first) and say which build the board holds when you stop.
68	
69	## Tools
70	
71	| Need | Use |
72	| --- | --- |
73	| Register a hack | `tools/wire_hack.py` |
74	| Flash a pinned build and read the serial log | `tools/flash_and_capture.sh`, `tools/serial_capture.py` |
75	| Does a test notice a break | `tools/mutate.py <file> 'old=>new' --cmd '...'` |
76	| Pin hashes | `HACK_PINS_OUT` (above) |
77

1	# Adding a hack
2	
3	Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md. The order of work is in `SKILL.md`.
4	
5	The `port-hack` skill orders this work, says what to read for before copying a
6	hack, and holds a recipe per trap. The steps:
7	
8	1. Check its row in `docs/porting-assessment.md` (effort and Speed band) and
9	   read its licence header.
10	2. Update the expected list in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` and see
11	   it fail. Add `test_<name>_stops_do_not_leak` beside the others, and
12	   mutation-check it: remove each free a wrapper adds and watch it fail.
13	3. Copy the file to `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/<name>.c`, add the notices row
14	   and an `extern` plus entry in `hacks/registry.c`.
15	4. Fill shim gaps test-first in `firmware/test/test_xshim/`. The compile
16	   check in `score_hacks.py` shows what is missing.
17	5. Host tests pass, dump a frame and look at it, then (with Rod's go-ahead)
18	   flash and measure fps and free heap/PSRAM over serial. To pin its frame
19	   hash after looking at the frame, put `0x1ull` in `kBaseline`, run
20	   `pio test -e native -f test_hacks`, convert the "Was N" in the failure line
21	   with `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"`, and run it again. A new hack never gets
22	   `0` in `kBaseline`: `0` is for a hack left unpinned on purpose, with the
23	   reason in its comment (DecayScreen, RotZoomer).
24	6. Regenerate the assessment and add measurements to
25	   `tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, then re-run the speed backtest: each port
26	   adds a point to the check of the Speed bands, which were fitted to the first
27	   29 hacks. To make a port a real test, commit its host time and predicted
28	   range first (`docs/speed-predictions.md` shows the form), flash it as copied,
29	   and add its name to `HOLDOUT` in `tools/speed_backtest.py`. The first four
30	   (Mountain, Epicycle, Kaleidescope, Celtic) all fell where predicted.
31	7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
32	   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (for a
33	   plain screenhack, `hacks/substrate_single.c`; the recipe is in the skill's
34	   `techniques.md`), and compare double and float frames at several frame
35	   counts. A resource
36	   override can skip a hack's restart cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so
37	   leak-test any override.
38	8. If Rod drops a port after seeing it (Hypnowheel, Boing; Celtic was dropped
39	   and came back through issue #37): remove it
40	   from `g_hacks[]`, the expected list, its hash and its leak test; keep the
41	   source and notices row; add `name: reason` (short: it is printed as a
42	   bullet) to `tools/failed_ports.txt`. For a GL hack, keep the `<name>_gl.c`
43	   wrapper but exclude it and the directory (`-<hacks/boing/>
44	   -<hacks/boing_gl.c>`) in all three `build_src_filter` lines, or it still
45	   builds. A reason Rod gave in his own words ("boring on a small screen") is
46	   the reason to record. File an issue only if there is something to come back
47	   to.
48	   Unhook its build steps too: its entry in `patch_float_literals.py` and any
49	   pre-script only it needs (BlockTube's `gl_textures.py`), or every build
50	   still runs them and fails without their `vendor/` input.
51	9. A header that a pre-script writes into the build dir (the font, the grab
52	   image) must be included under `__has_include` in `native/dump_main.c`:
53	   `tools/probe_hacks.py` compiles that file without the build's generated
54	   directory, and an unconditional include failed two `test_probe_hacks`
55	   cases. Add the pre-script to all three `extra_scripts` lines in
56	   `platformio.ini`, and a wrapper's original source to all three
57	   `build_src_filter` lines (`sed -i.bak 's|<last entry>$|<last entry> <new>|'`
58	   does all three).

# Porting assessment

Rough effort to port each xscreensaver hack to the StopWatch X11 shim,
generated from xscreensaver 6.17 by `tools/score_hacks.py`. Regenerate
it with `uv run tools/score_hacks.py`.

## How to read this

- **283 hacks** were scanned: every `hacks/*.c` and `hacks/glx/*.c`
  that registers itself with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`. Another 125
  files (3D models, helper libraries, command-line tools) are excluded and
  listed at the end.
- The scan is static and heuristic. For each 2D hack it counts the Xlib
  calls in the source that the shim does not declare, and it also
  syntax-checks the unmodified source against the shim's headers
  (`cc -fsyntax-only`). Anything the compiler cannot find is a **shim
  gap**: a missing header, type, struct field, constant or function.
  That second check catches helpers hacks reach through `utils/` that a
  count of Xlib calls cannot see. The effort rating does not run anything,
  so treat it as a prioritisation aid, not an estimate. It also says nothing
  about speed: see "Speed" below.
- The **All hacks** table lists the work still to do first, from least to
  most effort (S, M, L, XL) and then by name, and the ported hacks last.
  Its **Ported** column shows ✅ for a hack in the
  firmware's registry (`hacks/registry.c`) and ❌ for one that was
  attempted and abandoned (see "Failed ports" after the table, which only
  appears when there are any). Failures are recorded in
  `tools/failed_ports.txt`.

## Effort ratings

| Rating | Meaning | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S | 2D, and the unmodified source compiles against the shim | 3 |
| M | 2D, 1-4 shim gaps, no pixmaps or pixel read-back | 1 |
| L | 2D, 5+ shim gaps, or uses pixmaps or pixel read-back | 40 |
| XL | GL: runs on the TinyGL layer, each hack needs its own GL calls and helpers checked (see below) | 129 |
| Ported | Already running on the device, so no rating | 110 |

# Porting assessment

Rough effort to port each xscreensaver hack to the StopWatch X11 shim,
generated from xscreensaver 6.17 by `tools/score_hacks.py`. Regenerate
it with `uv run tools/score_hacks.py`.

## How to read this

- **283 hacks** were scanned: every `hacks/*.c` and `hacks/glx/*.c`
  that registers itself with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`. Another 125
  files (3D models, helper libraries, command-line tools) are excluded and
  listed at the end.
- The scan is static and heuristic. For each 2D hack it counts the Xlib
  calls in the source that the shim does not declare, and it also
  syntax-checks the unmodified source against the shim's headers
  (`cc -fsyntax-only`). Anything the compiler cannot find is a **shim
  gap**: a missing header, type, struct field, constant or function.
  That second check catches helpers hacks reach through `utils/` that a
  count of Xlib calls cannot see. The effort rating does not run anything,
  so treat it as a prioritisation aid, not an estimate. It also says nothing
  about speed: see "Speed" below.
- The **All hacks** table lists the work still to do first, from least to
  most effort (S, M, L, XL) and then by name, and the ported hacks last.
  Its **Ported** column shows ✅ for a hack in the
  firmware's registry (`hacks/registry.c`) and ❌ for one that was
  attempted and abandoned (see "Failed ports" after the table, which only
  appears when there are any). Failures are recorded in
  `tools/failed_ports.txt`.

## Effort ratings

| Rating | Meaning | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S | 2D, and the unmodified source compiles against the shim | 3 |
| M | 2D, 1-4 shim gaps, no pixmaps or pixel read-back | 1 |
| L | 2D, 5+ shim gaps, or uses pixmaps or pixel read-back | 40 |
| XL | GL: runs on the TinyGL layer, each hack needs its own GL calls and helpers checked (see below) | 129 |
| Ported | Already running on the device, so no rating | 110 |

# GL budget: cubicgrid and morph3d

`tools/gl_budget.py` runs a GL hack on the host, counts what each frame asks of
TinyGL, and predicts the device frame time. It was built to choose between two
candidates for the next GL port (issue #45) without flashing either.

```text
uv run tools/gl_budget.py [--frames N] [--seeds a,b,c]
    [--override '*name: value' ...] name[:seed] ...
```

Gears is read from `firmware/src/hacks/gears/`; any other name from
`vendor/xscreensaver-6.17/hacks/glx/` (git-ignored, never copied into the
repo). A hack that does not build is reported with its first error, and the
exit status is 1.

`--override` gives the hack a resource line that beats its own defaults, as an
entry in `registry.c`'s override list does on the device. Repeat it for more.
It applies to every hack named, so run hacks with different overrides
separately. Use it to try a registry override (`--override '*count: 40'`)
before committing to it, or to supply one a hack needs to start.

## What it counts

The counters sit inside a private copy of TinyGL, built only for the tool
(`firmware/src/tinygl/` and the firmware builds are untouched). Counting there
means a display list that is built once and replayed every frame is counted on
every frame. Per frame, it records:

- **Vertices** set up, and how many of them were lit.
- **Triangles** rasterised, after back-face culling, and the **pixels** they
  cover (screen area, overdraw included, capped at the canvas).
- **Lines** and **points** drawn.

## The cost model

A frame costs a fixed 56.6 ms (clear 24.6 ms, display push 32 ms), plus 4 us
per vertex, 2.8 us more for each enabled light on each lit vertex (both from the
Pipes probe in #43, measured with one light), plus a fill term. The fill term
is 570 ns a pixel, fitted so that the heavy Gears scene (seed 13, 17,700
vertices) costs the 40 ms of fill that #43 measured.

Checked against Gears, the only hack with device numbers. The fit and the
tests use 60 frames; the table below is a 300 frame run, and Gears' pixel
count drifts by about 15 percent between the two as the gears turn (at 60
frames the heavy scene is 217 ms and its fill is exactly 40 ms; at 300 it is
211 ms and 34 ms):

| Scene | Predicted | Measured (#43) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gears seed 13, heavy | 211 ms, 4.7 fps | 197 to 217 ms, about 5 fps |
| Gears seed 11, light (held out) | 117 ms, 8.5 fps | about 111 ms, 9 fps |

The light scene was not used in the fit and lands within 6 percent.

## The comparison

Means over 300 frames after a 10 frame warm-up. Both hacks are lit or point
based, so the fixed 56.6 ms sets a ceiling of about 17.7 fps for anything.

                    [--seeds SEEDS]

  hacks                 hack name, or name:seed to give it one seed

options:

"""PlatformIO pre-build script: converts the textures GL hacks load
(BlockTube's blocktube.png) into the raw blobs they include as
images/gen/<name>_png.h (see src/x11shim/include/ximage-loader.h for the
format), as matrix_glyphs.py does for XMatrix, and puts them on the include
path. The images are read from vendor/ and never committed. Needs uv, because
Pillow is not in PlatformIO's Python."""

import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

Import("env")  # noqa: F821

repo = Path(env["PROJECT_DIR"]).parent  # noqa: F821
sys.path.insert(0, str(repo / "tools"))
import xs_vendor

images = xs_vendor.upstream(repo) / "hacks" / "images"
converter = repo / "tools" / "make_logo_blob.py"
generated = Path(env.subst("$BUILD_DIR")) / "generated"  # noqa: F821

for name in ("blocktube",):
    image = images / f"{name}.png"
    header = generated / "images" / "gen" / f"{name}_png.h"
    if not image.is_file():
        sys.exit(f"{image} is missing: run `uv run tools/fetch_xscreensaver.py`")
    if (
        header.exists()
        and header.stat().st_mtime >= image.stat().st_mtime
        and header.stat().st_mtime >= converter.stat().st_mtime
    ):
        continue
    uv = shutil.which("uv")
    if not uv:
        raise SystemExit("gl_textures.py needs uv on PATH to convert the textures")
    header.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    # Written beside the header and renamed, so a killed build never leaves a
    # truncated header that the mtime check above would trust.
    partial = header.with_name(header.name + ".partial")
    partial.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    subprocess.run(
        [
            uv,
            "run",
            str(converter),
            str(image),
            "--name",
            f"{name}_png",
            "-o",
            str(partial),
        ],
        check=True,
    )
    os.replace(partial, header)

env.Append(CPPPATH=[str(generated)])  # noqa: F821
  numbers are double the device's.
- Plain `malloc` and `realloc` of two 868 KB buffers (Substrate) landed in
  PSRAM: free PSRAM fell by 1,742,096 bytes, which is 2 x 466 x 466 x 4 plus a
  few KB. Internal heap barely moved.
- On restart the buffers were freed and allocated again, and free PSRAM
  returned to the same value. Read heap and PSRAM in the log to confirm this
  for each large hack.

## Images

Colour pixmaps are canvases: every drawing primitive, `XCopyArea` and
`XCopyPlane` draw into them. Bitmaps take only `XCopyArea` from another
bitmap. There is no PNG
decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads a raw RGB565 blob and
mask (format in `ximage-loader.h`), made by `tools/make_logo_blob.py`.
`XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repository root) swaps the logo for a local
image at build time. Keep a third-party logo under `vendor/`, out of git.

A big blob (Pacman's is 3 MB as C text) is built from `vendor/` by a `pre:`
script and never committed; write it to a `.partial` file and rename it.

## Pixmap double buffering

When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)

- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.

## Restart leak test

When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.

Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.

On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.

## Stopping before the first draw

When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
frames exited 139.

- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).

## Tests that cannot be fooled

A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.

A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
old start.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/worktree-session

# Working in a git worktree

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- In a git worktree the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/` are
  missing. Symlink them from the main checkout. `.gitignore`'s trailing slashes
  don't match symlinks, so they would show as untracked, but the shared
  `.git/info/exclude` already lists the three names. That file is shared by
  every worktree: ask Rod before adding to it.
  The harness refuses `source tools/env.sh` and a computed `PATH` there: run
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio ...` instead,
  and keep commands plain (no scripts, loops, `$VAR` in a command or `&&`
  chains with a computed path). A worktree an agent works in (`isolation:
  "worktree"`) starts from `origin/main`, not from your branch, and has no
  vendor or toolchain until you link them.
  It also refuses heredocs, `git -C` and `cd` into another worktree: use the
  Edit and Write tools. It refuses `git ... | tar` and `cd <dir> && git ...`
  too: use `git archive -o f.tar <sha>` then `tar -x -f f.tar -C <dir>`, and run
  git from the worktree root. A background shell starts there as well, so use
  `pio test -d <abs>/firmware` with absolute paths. Parallel calls can race
  (a `uv run` in the root disturbed `.venv` while `pio` ran:
  "../.venv/bin/pio: no such file"), so run
  `uv` and `pio` one at a time. To fast-forward `main` or remove the worktree,
  leave it first with `ExitWorktree keep`. If no checkout has `main` out,
  `git fetch origin main:main` fast-forwards it from anywhere.
  Before `ExitWorktree remove` on a merged branch, check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main`; the tool's "discarded N
  commits" count ignores merges. `.platformio`, `.venv` and `vendor` there are
  symlinks, so removal leaves the real ones alone. After a merge,
  `ExitWorktree keep` names a branch (`worktree-<name>`) that may not exist:
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` and delete the
  real branch, as separate commands, because a failed `&&` link skips the rest
  silently. Check `git worktree list` afterwards. `git worktree remove --force`
  fails on a worktree this session's harness locked ("cannot remove a locked
  working tree, lock reason: claude session"): once the tip is an ancestor of
  `origin/main`, `ExitWorktree remove` with `discard_changes: true` works, and
  its "discarded N commits" are the merged ones. In a session resumed from a
  summary, `ExitWorktree` can be a no-op ("no active EnterWorktree session"):
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` from the main
  checkout instead. To delete the merged branch
  you are standing on, `git switch --detach origin/main` in the worktree first.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort.
