tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Biggest lessons: (1) TinyGL has no alpha, so a hack that keeps its look in alpha (GLMatrix, DeepStars) needs alpha folded into colour in a wrapper; glshim.h defines glTexImage2D as a macro, so include xlockmore.h BEFORE redefining it. (5) Hack *delay credited only against push: a 10 ms override gave +40-70% fps on delay-paced hacks. (6) The restart leak test found a real upstream leak in cubenetic.

content.text:
I ported eight GL hacks, GL Matrix included. The two commits are on `feature/gl-batch-7-glmatrix`, local only: nothing is pushed and there's no PR, since you didn't ask for one.

**What each one does on the board** (one 45 s rotation lap, eight windows each):

| Hack | fps range | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GLMatrix | 13-44 | about 17 once the screen is full; 6 as copied |
| CubeStack | 17-38 | |
| Kaleidocycle | 30-35 | |
| DangerBall | 24-26 | |
| Cubenetic | 12-18 | 1.2 fps as copied |
| DeepStars | 18-20 | 3-10 fps as copied |
| Superquadrics | 14-27 | 8-11 fps as copied |
| Menger | 13-44 | |

**GL Matrix:** it was the hard one. TinyGL has no alpha, and GL Matrix keeps its glyph shape and brightness in alpha, so at first every glyph was a solid green square. The wrapper now folds the alpha into the colour; an additive blend can't tell the difference. The remaining cost was fill, so it renders at half size with `*density: 12` and a 10 ms delay. It's chunkier than full size, and `-DGLMATRIX_FULL` restores full size at about 7 fps.

**Other fixes:**
- **Cubenetic** recomputed a 256×256 plasma texture every frame (847 ms). It's now 64×64 via a build-time patch.
- **Superquadrics and Menger** were black because TinyGL draws nothing for `GL_POLYGON` (issue #80). Each wrapper draws the quads as triangle fans, as Rubik does, and both render at half size. Menger's `*maxDepth` is capped at 2, because depth 3 took 920 ms a frame.
- **DeepStars** folds alpha into colour too. Its `*smear` is capped at 4, since upstream grows it to 400 copies of 2,700 stars (3.4 fps at 20). Its stars are dim by design.
- The three delay-paced hacks (CubeStack, Kaleidocycle, DangerBall) gained 30-70% from a 10 ms delay override alone.
- **A real upstream leak:** Cubenetic never frees its cube array (320 bytes a start). The restart leak test found it, and the wrapper now frees it.

**Verification:**
- **Host suite:** all 860 pass.
- **Mutation checks:** the mutations I tried on the new wrappers were caught.
- **Soak:** a 14-minute rotation at 5 s a hack showed no resets or panics. PSRAM and heap were identical on the second visit of each new hack.
- **FMA run:** with `-ffp-contract=off` the `test_hacks` run stops at XSpirograph, an older hack I didn't touch. The new pins weren't reached under that setting, and I didn't check whether main fails the same way.

**For you to look at:** the board is flashed with a rotating build (90 s per hack) that starts on GL Matrix. Only you can judge it by eye, mainly GL Matrix at half size and whether DeepStars is too dim.

**Not done:**
- **Cage and Moebius:** they need `e_textures.h` and a wood texture.
- **Shared `GL_POLYGON` fix:** two wrappers now work around issue #80 locally. A proper fix in the shared GL layer is your call.
- **Setup:** I worked on a plain branch in the main checkout rather than a worktree, as nothing else was using it.

Want me to push and open a draft PR?

cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-rod-build-stopwatch-screensaver/affddb2d-bfaf-4405-b4b6-244f3afec578/scratchpad/issue.md <<'EOF'
TinyGL here is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), so a hack that calls `glBegin(GL_POLYGON)` draws nothing. Issue #80 fixed `GL_LINE_LOOP` (which the same switch compiled out) and left polygons as "each hack works round it".

## Current state

Three wrappers map it to a triangle fan locally:

- `hacks/rubik_gl.c` (with a polygon offset for its decals)
- `hacks/menger_gl.c`
- `hacks/superquadrics_single_gl.c`

`buildlwo.c` (Pipes) does the same in its own wrapper. Without the mapping Menger and Superquadrics render black (found in the 2026-10-18 GL batch).

## Why a proper fix

The same `glBegin` macro is copied into every wrapper, and every unported GL hack that uses `GL_POLYGON` will hit it: circuit, dolphin, maze3d, polytopes, polyhedra-gl, shark, sonar, sproingies, topblock, whale. A hack that nobody wraps just draws black, and the host tests only notice if the hack has a "draws something" check.

## Options

1. Patch TinyGL (`tools/tinygl_patch.py`) to handle `GL_POLYGON` itself, as a fan from the first vertex. Exact for convex polygons, which is every use I have seen in the vendored hacks. Needs the same guard as the line loop patch, so an unhandled primitive cannot overrun the vertex slots.
2. Map it in `glshim.h` (`glBegin` to a shim function), so each hack gets it with no wrapper. Simplest, but changes what every GL hack sees, so it needs Rod's say.
3. Leave it per wrapper (today's state).

## Things to settle

- Non-convex polygons: a fan is wrong for them. Check each user in the list above for concave shapes before relying on it.
- Display lists: Menger records its quads in a list, so the mapping has to apply at record time as well as at draw time.
- Rubik's decals need a polygon offset on top of the fan, which should stay in its wrapper.
- Tests: a frame test per hack that draws only polygons (Superquadrics and Menger have one now), and a `test_glshim` case for a quad and a pentagon, mutation-checked.
- Once it is fixed, delete the three local mappings and the comment in `gl.md` that explains them.
EOF

content.text:
I filed the `GL_POLYGON` ticket as [#138](https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/138) and took DeepStars out of the rotation.

**Ticket #138:**
- **Problem:** four wrappers now map `GL_POLYGON` to a triangle fan locally. They are Rubik, Menger, Superquadrics and the Pipes helper. Ten other unported GL hacks use it and would draw black.
- **Options:** patch TinyGL (`tools/tinygl_patch.py`) to handle it as a fan, map it in `glshim.h`, or leave it per wrapper. The shim route changes what every GL hack sees, so it needs your say.
- **Things to settle:** non-convex polygons, display lists (Menger records its quads in one), and Rubik's decal offset.

**DeepStars:**
- **Cause:** I think the faint stars come from TinyGL having no real alpha or smooth points. Upstream's stars are dim (0.15-0.45) and only 0.5-3 px across, and I didn't find a way round that in the wrapper. I didn't look into the missing smear.
- **What was removed:** its registry entry, expected name, pinned hash and leak test. I added a line to `failed_ports.txt`.
- **What stays:** the source, wrapper and notices row, with the wrapper left out of the build filter. Bringing it back is documented in `hacks.md`.

**Checks:**
- **Tests:** the host hack tests pass (138 of 138).
- **Docs and tools:** the assessment is regenerated and the tools tests and notices check pass.
- **Commit:** `2040bd7` is on `feature/gl-batch-7-glmatrix`, local only, as before.

The board is flashed with this tree (rotating, starting on GL Matrix), so the rotation now has seven new hacks. I didn't re-measure after the removal.

Want me to push and open a draft PR now?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/deliver-branch

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `entire trail merge <trail>` (the trail
  number, not the PR number; omit it on the trail's branch) once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). `entire trail merge` checks the gates first and
  merges nothing while one fails or is pending; `--dry-run` reports which.
  Rod's approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire Gates check to finish.
  If the only failing gates are Approvals (he approved in chat) or a stacked
  PR's "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges, and the PR is
  mergeable, try `entire trail merge <trail> --force --yes` with no rebase;
  the bypass is recorded on the trail. The repo's bypass policy is now
  "nobody", so it is refused ("does not allow bypassing gates", PR #132):
  do not merge round it with `gh pr merge`. Ask Rod to approve the trail in
  the Entire UI, then run a plain `entire trail merge`. For any other failing
  gate, stop and tell Rod.

Written by an agent (Claude) running under Rod's direction.

## What this adds

Seven GL hacks on the TinyGL layer, each the unmodified xscreensaver source
built through a `USE_GL` wrapper: GLMatrix, CubeStack, Kaleidocycle,
DangerBall, Cubenetic, Superquadrics and Menger. DeepStars was ported too, and
Rod dropped it after seeing it on the panel (about three dim stars, no smear);
its source, wrapper and notices row stay, and it is in `failed_ports.txt`.

| Hack | On the board (45 s windows) | Wrapper work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GLMatrix | 13-44 fps, about 17 once full (6 as copied) | alpha folded into colour, half size, density 12, 10 ms delay, single precision |
| CubeStack | 17-38 fps | 10 ms delay |
| Kaleidocycle | 30-35 fps | 10 ms delay |
| DangerBall | 24-26 fps | 10 ms delay |
| Cubenetic | 12-18 fps (1.2 as copied) | 64 by 64 texture, single precision, frees its cube array |
| Superquadrics | 14-27 fps (8-11 as copied) | triangle fans for `GL_POLYGON`, half size, single precision |
| Menger | 13-44 fps | triangle fans for `GL_POLYGON`, half size, `*maxDepth: 2` |

## Notes for review

- GLMatrix keeps its look in alpha, which TinyGL lacks. The wrapper
  premultiplies the glyph texture as it uploads and scales `glColor4f`; an
  additive blend cannot tell the difference. `matrix3.png` is deflated at build
  time by `gl_textures.py`, never committed.
- Cubenetic's plasma texture was 847 ms a frame at 256 by 256.
  `tools/cubenetic_patch.py` makes the size a build setting (64 by 64).
- The restart leak test found a real upstream leak in Cubenetic (320 bytes a
  start); the wrapper frees it.
- Superquadrics and Menger drew nothing because TinyGL has no `GL_POLYGON`
  (issue #80). Each wrapper draws a fan, as Rubik does. A shared fix is filed
  as #138; I did not touch the shared GL layer.
- Registry overrides: `*delay: 10000` for the six that were paced by their own
  delay (the loop credits only the push against it), `*density: 12` for
  GLMatrix, `*maxDepth: 2` for Menger.
- Menger's frame rate swings 13-44 fps: the low end is while a depth level's
  display list is built.

## Verified

- Host: `pio test -e native` passes, 860 of 860, before DeepStars was dropped;
  after it, `test_hacks` passes, 138 of 138. `uv run pytest tools/tests` and
  `check_notices.py` pass.
- Pinned frame hashes were taken after looking at the frames. Mutation checks
  were caught: GLMatrix's alpha and colour folds, both polygon-fan mappings,
  and Cubenetic's free.
- Device: flashed and measured with `flash_and_capture.sh`, one 45 s lap for
  the numbers above, then a 14 minute soak at 5 s a hack: no reset, panic or
  stack canary, and PSRAM and heap identical on the second visit of each.

## Not verified

- Only Rod can say what the panel shows. In particular GLMatrix at half size
  is chunkier than full size (`-DGLMATRIX_FULL` restores it, at about 7 fps).
- `test_hacks` with `-ffp-contract=off` stops at XSpirograph, an older hack, so
  the new pins were not checked that way. I did not check whether main fails
  the same way.
- The full native suite was not re-run after DeepStars was dropped (only
  `test_hacks`, the tools tests and the notices check).
- GLMatrix's additive blend double-draws the shared diagonal of each quad
  (TinyGL's inclusive edges); I did not see it in the frames and did not
  measure it.
- Cage and Moebius were left out: they need `e_textures.h` and a wood texture.

Refs #80, #138.

The PR body says it was written by an agent under your direction. It has the per-hack fps table and the review notes. It also lists what's unverified:

- Only you can judge the panel, especially GLMatrix at half size.
- `-ffp-contract=off` stops at XSpirograph, so the new pins weren't checked that way.
- I only re-ran `test_hacks` after dropping DeepStars, not the full native suite.
- GLMatrix's additive blend may double-draw quad diagonals; I didn't see it in the frames or measure it.
- Cage and Moebius were left out.

It refs #80 and #138 rather than closing anything, so no `Fixes #N` line. I haven't run the review findings or the merge, since you approve and merge. Tell me when you want that.

Filed by an agent (Claude) for Rod.

`AGENTS.md` says to run the suite both ways when float code is involved (a pinned hash can fail under `-ffp-contract=off`). Running it that way on the GL batch branch (PR #139) stopped at XSpirograph, which that branch does not touch.

## What happened

From `firmware/`:

```text
REDACTED NO_COLOR=1 pio test -e native -f test_hacks
```

Result: 140 cases, 1 failed.

```text
test_hacks.c:613: test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main:
  Expected 15412848725209834749 Was 16303972679858120643. XSpirograph [FAILED]
```

The same suite without the flag passes (860 of 860 across the native suite). That test stops at the first moved hash in registry order, so every hack after XSpirograph is hidden behind it, including any pins that would also move.

## Not known

- Whether `main` fails the same way. I did not run it there, so this may be old, not something the branch caused.
- Which other hacks' pins move under the flag. See the gotcha in `AGENTS.md` about listing them all (temporarily append `name idx got=0x...` to a buffer and `TEST_FAIL_MESSAGE` it, then `git checkout` the file).

2. List every pin that moves with `-ffp-contract=off` (the buffer trick above).
3. For each, decide: a hash that depends on FMA contraction should be a comparison against a reference copy (as the `canvas_line` and clip tests do), not a pinned hash; or the pin is a real difference in the frame.
4. Say in `AGENTS.md` whether running both ways is still expected of a port, since it cannot be if main fails it.

I've filed it as [#140](https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/140), "Pinned frame hashes move under -ffp-contract=off (XSpirograph first)".

It records the command and the failing assertion, with the expected and actual hashes. It also says the test stops at the first moved hash, so every hack after XSpirograph is hidden behind it. I didn't run it on `main`, so the issue says plainly that it may be an old problem and not something the GL branch caused.

The to-do list in the issue is:
1. Run the same command on `main`.
2. List every pin that moves, using the buffer trick from `AGENTS.md`.
3. Decide, for each pin that moves, whether to replace the pinned hash with a comparison against a reference copy.
4. Update the guidance in `AGENTS.md` about running the suite both ways.

I haven't linked it from the PR body. I can add a "Refs #140" line to #139 if you want it there.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

Two open findings on trail 83, both fixed and resolved on the trail. Nothing is committed: the changes are in the working tree for your review, as the skill requires.

**Resolved via manual edit** (neither finding had a suggested patch):

- **CubeStack drew faces at full brightness instead of fading** (`cubestack_gl.c`). The review was right: CubeStack blends `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE` with a per-face alpha, and TinyGL ignores vertex alpha. The wrapper's `glColor4fv` now scales its colour by alpha, as GLMatrix's does. A new test checks the first frame is black; before the fix it lit 10,883 pixels, exactly as the review said. The cubes are now translucent, as upstream draws them. I looked at the frames before re-pinning the hash (now `0x863e3b620c76d7e1`).
- **Palette index overflow** (`cubestack_gl.c`). Upstream wraps `ccolor` with `>` instead of `>=`, so after about 12,900 frames it reads `colors[32]` of a 32-entry array. A new 13,500-frame test hit the AddressSanitizer heap-buffer-overflow before the fix. The wrapper now wraps the index before each draw, and the copied hack stays byte-identical.

**Checks:**
- **Tests:** `test_hacks` passes (140 of 140).
- **Mutations:** both are caught. Removing the alpha scaling fails the pinned frame, and I saw the dedicated alpha test fail on its own earlier. Reverting the wrap aborts under AddressSanitizer.
- **Board:** CubeStack measured 17-20 fps in a 50 s capture with the fix. The board is reflashed with the rotating build that starts on GL Matrix.
- **Docs:** I added a CubeStack note to `.claude/rules/hacks.md`.

**Not fixed:** Kaleidocycle also sets a blend, but its faces are opaque, so I left it alone.

Want me to commit and push these to #139?

content.thinking: The upstream `myrand` also rounds 2147483647 up to 2147483648 due to the float conversion in `(float) range * LRAND()`. I'll write a test reproducing this with a stub returning that value, then fix it via the same build-time patch approach used for the other wrappers.

input.command:
cat > tools/superquadrics_patch.py <<'EOF'
"""Keeps Superquadrics's random index below its range.

Upstream's `myrand` multiplies in `float`, so the largest value `LRAND()` can
return (2147483647) rounds up to 2^31 and `myrand(4)` is 4, which then indexes
`pats[4][t]` in a 4 by 4 array. The build (firmware/patch_float_literals.py)
runs this on the hack's text; the copied superquadrics.c stays byte-identical.
The replacement is checked, so a change upstream fails the build.
"""

OLD = "\treturn ((int) (((float) range) * LRAND() / (MAXRAND)));\n"
NEW = (
    "\tint r = (int) (((float) range) * LRAND() / (MAXRAND));\n"
    "\treturn r < range ? r : range - 1;\n"
)


def keep_myrand_in_range(source: str) -> str:
    found = source.count(OLD)
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 of `{OLD.strip()}` in superquadrics.c, found {found}; "
            "has upstream changed?"
        )
    return source.replace(OLD, NEW)
EOF
cat > tools/tests/test_superquadrics_patch.py <<'EOF'
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

import superquadrics_patch as sp
import xs_vendor

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
UPSTREAM = xs_vendor.upstream(ROOT) / "hacks" / "glx" / "superquadrics.c"

SAMPLE = """\
static int
myrand(int range)
{
\treturn ((int) (((float) range) * LRAND() / (MAXRAND)));
}
"""


def test_the_random_index_is_clamped():
    out = sp.keep_myrand_in_range(SAMPLE)
    assert "return r < range ? r : range - 1;" in out
    assert "((float) range) * LRAND()" in out


def test_it_refuses_a_source_that_has_changed():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="upstream"):
        sp.keep_myrand_in_range(SAMPLE.replace("(float) range", "(double) range"))


def _myrand_at_the_top_of_the_range(tmp_path: Path, source: str, range_: int) -> int:
    body = re.search(r"static int\nmyrand\(int range\)\n\{.*?\n\}\n", source, re.S)
    assert body
    program = (
        "#include <stdio.h>\n"
        "#define LRAND() 2147483647L\n"
        "#define MAXRAND (2147483648.0)\n"
        f"{body.group(0)}"
        f'int main(void) {{ printf("%d", myrand({range_})); return 0; }}\n'
    )
    c = tmp_path / "myrand.c"
    c.write_text(program)
    exe = tmp_path / "myrand"
    subprocess.run(["cc", "-o", str(exe), str(c)], check=True)
    return int(subprocess.run([str(exe)], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout)


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
@pytest.mark.parametrize("range_", [2, 3, 4, 100, 200])

content.text:
The Superquadrics finding is fixed and marked resolved on trail 83. Nothing is committed yet.

- **Cause:** the reviewer was right, and upstream has it too. `myrand` multiplies in `float`, so when `LRAND()` returns 2147483647 it rounds up to 2147483648 and `myrand(4)` returns 4. `MakeUpStuff` then reads one row past the end of `pats[4][4]`.
- **Fix:** `tools/superquadrics_patch.py` clamps the result below `range` at build time. The build runs it through `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, so the copied hack stays byte-identical. The generated source has the clamp. I checked that by reading the generated file, not by running a frame.
- **Test:** `tools/tests/test_superquadrics_patch.py` compiles the real `myrand` with `LRAND()` fixed at 2147483647. Upstream's version returns 4 there, which reproduces the bug, and the patched version returns `range - 1` for ranges 2, 3, 4, 100 and 200. Reverting the clamp makes the test fail. I wrote the patch and the test together, so I didn't watch the test fail before the fix, but the upstream check shows the bug.
- **Checks:** `test_hacks` passes (140 of 140) and the tools tests pass (612). The frame pins didn't move.
- **Docs:** I added a line to `.claude/rules/hacks.md`.

I didn't flash the board, since only the build path changed and the clamp can't alter a frame unless the random value is the one-in-two-billion case.

Changes are in the working tree (`hacks.md`, `patch_float_literals.py` and the two new files). Want me to commit and push them to #139?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

cat > tools/glmatrix_patch.py <<'EOF'
"""Keeps GLMatrix's brightness wave index inside its table.

Upstream indexes `brightness_ramp[WAVE_SIZE]` with
`WAVE_SIZE - ((i + (GRID_SIZE - wave_position)) % WAVE_SIZE)`, which runs from
1 to WAVE_SIZE: a zero remainder reads one entry past the table, into the next
screen's state. The index counts down through the wave and the entry after 1 is
0, so the patch wraps WAVE_SIZE to 0. The build (firmware/patch_float_literals.py)
runs this on the hack's text; the copied glmatrix.c stays byte-identical. The
replacement is checked, so a change upstream fails the build.
"""

import re

OLD = re.compile(
    r"int j = WAVE_SIZE - \(\(i \+ \(GRID_SIZE - s->wave_position\)\)\s*% WAVE_SIZE\);"
)
NEW = (
    "int j = (WAVE_SIZE - ((i + (GRID_SIZE - s->wave_position)) % WAVE_SIZE))"
    " % WAVE_SIZE;"
)


def keep_the_wave_index_in_range(source: str) -> str:
    found = len(OLD.findall(source))
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 brightness wave index in glmatrix.c, found {found}; "
            "has upstream changed?"
        )
    return OLD.sub(NEW, source)
EOF

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

import glmatrix_patch as gp
import xs_vendor

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
UPSTREAM = xs_vendor.upstream(ROOT) / "hacks" / "glx" / "glmatrix.c"

SAMPLE = """\
          int j = WAVE_SIZE - ((i + (GRID_SIZE - s->wave_position))
                               % WAVE_SIZE);
          brightness = mp->brightness_ramp[j];
"""


def test_the_wave_index_wraps_to_zero():
    out = gp.keep_the_wave_index_in_range(SAMPLE)
    assert "% WAVE_SIZE)) % WAVE_SIZE;" in out
    assert "brightness = mp->brightness_ramp[j];" in out


def test_it_refuses_a_source_that_has_changed():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="upstream"):
        gp.keep_the_wave_index_in_range(SAMPLE.replace("GRID_SIZE", "GRID_WIDTH"))


def _wave_indexes(tmp_path: Path, source: str) -> list[int]:
    """Every index the hack's own statement gives, over each row of the grid and
    each wave position, by compiling that statement with the hack's constants."""
    wave = re.search(r"#define WAVE_SIZE\s+(\d+)", source)
    grid = re.search(r"#define GRID_SIZE\s+(\d+)", source)
    stmt = re.search(r"int j = WAVE_SIZE - .*?;", source, re.S)
    assert wave and grid and stmt
    program = (
        "#include <stdio.h>\n"
        f"#define WAVE_SIZE {wave[1]}\n"
        f"#define GRID_SIZE {grid[1]}\n"
        "struct S { int wave_position; };\n"
        "int main(void) {\n"
        "  struct S st, *s = &st;\n"
        f"  for (int wp = 0; wp < WAVE_SIZE; wp++) {{ st.wave_position = wp;\n"
        "    for (int i = 0; i < GRID_SIZE; i++) {\n"
        f"      {stmt.group(0)}\n"
        '      printf("%d\\n", j);\n'
        "    } }\n"
        "  return 0; }\n"
    )
    c = tmp_path / "wave.c"
    c.write_text(program)
    exe = tmp_path / "wave"
    subprocess.run(["cc", "-o", str(exe), str(c)], check=True)
    out = subprocess.run([str(exe)], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return [int(x) for x in out.stdout.split()]


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
def test_patched_indexes_stay_inside_the_table(tmp_path):
    source = UPSTREAM.read_text()
    size = int(re.search(r"#define WAVE_SIZE\s+(\d+)", source)[1])
    indexes = _wave_indexes(tmp_path, gp.keep_the_wave_index_in_range(source))
    assert min(indexes) == 0 and max(indexes) == size - 1


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
def test_upstream_reaches_one_past_the_table(tmp_path):
    source = UPSTREAM.read_text()
    size = int(re.search(r"#define WAVE_SIZE\s+(\d+)", source)[1])
    assert max(_wave_indexes(tmp_path, source)) == size
EOF

"""Keeps GLMatrix's brightness wave index inside its table.

Upstream indexes `brightness_ramp[WAVE_SIZE]` with
`WAVE_SIZE - ((i + (GRID_SIZE - wave_position)) % WAVE_SIZE)`, which runs from
1 to WAVE_SIZE: a zero remainder reads one entry past the table, into the next
screen's state. The index counts down through the wave and the entry after 1 is
0, so the patch wraps WAVE_SIZE to 0. The build (firmware/patch_float_literals.py)
runs this on the hack's text; the copied glmatrix.c stays byte-identical. The
replacement is checked, so a change upstream fails the build.
"""

import re

OLD = re.compile(
    r"int j = WAVE_SIZE - \(\(i \+ \(GRID_SIZE - s->wave_position\)\)\s*% WAVE_SIZE\);"
)
NEW = (
    "int j = (WAVE_SIZE - ((i + (GRID_SIZE - s->wave_position)) % WAVE_SIZE))"
    " % WAVE_SIZE;"
)


def keep_the_wave_index_in_range(source: str) -> str:
    found = len(OLD.findall(source))
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 brightness wave index in glmatrix.c, found {found}; "
            "has upstream changed?"
        )
    return OLD.sub(NEW, source)
EOF

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

import glmatrix_patch as gp
import xs_vendor

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
UPSTREAM = xs_vendor.upstream(ROOT) / "hacks" / "glx" / "glmatrix.c"

SAMPLE = """\
          int j = WAVE_SIZE - ((i + (GRID_SIZE - s->wave_position))
                               % WAVE_SIZE);
          brightness = mp->brightness_ramp[j];
"""


def test_the_wave_index_wraps_to_zero():
    out = gp.keep_the_wave_index_in_range(SAMPLE)
    assert "% WAVE_SIZE)) % WAVE_SIZE;" in out
    assert "brightness = mp->brightness_ramp[j];" in out


def test_it_refuses_a_source_that_has_changed():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="upstream"):
        gp.keep_the_wave_index_in_range(SAMPLE.replace("GRID_SIZE", "GRID_WIDTH"))


def _wave_indexes(tmp_path: Path, source: str) -> list[int]:
    """Every index the hack's own statement gives, over each row of the grid and
    each wave position, by compiling that statement with the hack's constants."""
    wave = re.search(r"#define WAVE_SIZE\s+(\d+)", source)
    grid = re.search(r"#define GRID_SIZE\s+(\d+)", source)
    stmt = re.search(r"int j = WAVE_SIZE - .*?;", source, re.S)
    assert wave and grid and stmt
    program = (
        "#include <stdio.h>\n"
        f"#define WAVE_SIZE {wave[1]}\n"
        f"#define GRID_SIZE {grid[1]}\n"
        "struct S { int wave_position; };\n"
        "int main(void) {\n"
        "  struct S st, *s = &st;\n"
        f"  for (int wp = 0; wp < WAVE_SIZE; wp++) {{ st.wave_position = wp;\n"
        "    for (int i = 0; i < GRID_SIZE; i++) {\n"
        f"      {stmt.group(0)}\n"
        '      printf("%d\\n", j);\n'
        "    } }\n"
        "  return 0; }\n"
    )
    c = tmp_path / "wave.c"
    c.write_text(program)
    exe = tmp_path / "wave"
    subprocess.run(["cc", "-o", str(exe), str(c)], check=True)
    out = subprocess.run([str(exe)], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return [int(x) for x in out.stdout.split()]


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
def test_patched_indexes_stay_inside_the_table(tmp_path):
    source = UPSTREAM.read_text()
    size = int(re.search(r"#define WAVE_SIZE\s+(\d+)", source)[1])
    indexes = _wave_indexes(tmp_path, gp.keep_the_wave_index_in_range(source))
    assert min(indexes) == 0 and max(indexes) == size - 1


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
def test_upstream_reaches_one_past_the_table(tmp_path):
    source = UPSTREAM.read_text()
    size = int(re.search(r"#define WAVE_SIZE\s+(\d+)", source)[1])
    assert max(_wave_indexes(tmp_path, source)) == size
EOF

content.text:
Entire Address Findings:

The one open finding is fixed and marked resolved on trail 83. Nothing is committed.

**Resolved via manual edit** (the finding had no suggested patch): the GLMatrix brightness wave index (`glmatrix.c:469`, medium).

- **Cause:** the reviewer was right. Upstream computes `WAVE_SIZE - (… % WAVE_SIZE)`, which runs 1 to 22, and the ramp table has 22 entries (0 to 21). A zero remainder read one past the end, into the next screen's state. On the board that meant an occasional glyph at a junk brightness.
- **Fix:** `tools/glmatrix_patch.py` wraps the index to 0. The build applies it through `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, so the copied hack stays byte-identical. The generated source has the change. Wrapping to 0 is the natural continuation of the cycle: the index counts down, so after 1 comes 0, which is the brightest entry.
- **Test:** `tools/tests/test_glmatrix_patch.py` compiles the hack's own statement over every row and wave position. Upstream reaches index 22, which reproduces the overflow. The patched version stays within 0 to 21. Breaking the wrap is caught.
- **Pin:** GLMatrix's pinned hash moved, as expected, since the out-of-bounds read had been changing the frame. I looked at the new frame (clear glyph rain) and re-took the pin (`0x9b9fab38bc9ac1a1`).
- **Checks:** `test_hacks` passes (140 of 140) and the tools tests pass (616).
- **Board:** a 100 s capture ran at 16-17 fps, as before. The board is back on the rotating build that starts on GL Matrix.
- **Docs:** I added a note to `.claude/rules/hacks.md`.

**Changed files:**
- `.claude/rules/hacks.md`
- `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`
- `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c`
- `tools/glmatrix_patch.py` (new)
- `tools/tests/test_glmatrix_patch.py` (new)

Want me to commit and push them to #139?

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.

cd /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver && cat > tools/kaleidocycle_patch.py <<'EOF'
"""Keeps Kaleidocycle's first frame from dividing zero by zero.

The hack starts with `bp->count = 0` and the piece loop runs once at that
count, so its rotation `(i/2) * 4 * 180 / bp->count` is 0 / 0: a NaN angle that
reaches TinyGL's viewport conversion and is cast to an int (undefined; found by
the trail review with -fsanitize=float-cast-overflow). The build
(firmware/patch_float_literals.py) runs this on the hack's text; the copied
kaleidocycle.c stays byte-identical. The replacement is checked, so a change
upstream fails the build.
"""

OLD = "glRotatef ((i/2) * 4 * 180 / bp->count, 0, 0, 1);"
NEW = "glRotatef ((i/2) * 4 * 180 / (bp->count > 0 ? bp->count : 1), 0, 0, 1);"


def guard_the_zero_count(source: str) -> str:
    found = source.count(OLD)
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 of `{OLD}` in kaleidocycle.c, found {found}; "
            "has upstream changed?"
        )
    return source.replace(OLD, NEW)
EOF
cat > tools/tests/test_kaleidocycle_patch.py <<'EOF'
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

import kaleidocycle_patch as kp
import xs_vendor

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
UPSTREAM = xs_vendor.upstream(ROOT) / "hacks" / "glx" / "kaleidocycle.c"

SAMPLE = """\
      glPushMatrix();
      glRotatef ((i/2) * 4 * 180 / bp->count, 0, 0, 1);
      if (flip_p) reflect (-sin(a), cos(a), 0);
"""


def test_the_count_is_guarded():
    out = kp.guard_the_zero_count(SAMPLE)
    assert "/ (bp->count > 0 ? bp->count : 1), 0, 0, 1);" in out
    assert "if (flip_p) reflect" in out


def test_it_refuses_a_source_that_has_changed():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="upstream"):
        kp.guard_the_zero_count(SAMPLE.replace("180", "360"))


def _first_angle_at_count_zero(tmp_path: Path, source: str) -> str:
    """The angle the hack's own glRotatef call gets for piece 0 at count 0."""
    call = re.search(r"glRotatef \(\(i/2\).*?, 0, 0, 1\);", source)
    assert call
    program = (
        "#include <stdio.h>\n"
        "static void glRotatef(float a, float x, float y, float z) {\n"
        '  printf("%f", a); (void)x; (void)y; (void)z; }\n'
        "struct B { float count; };\n"
        "int main(void) { struct B b = {0}, *bp = &b; int i = 0;\n"
        f"  {call.group(0)}\n"
        "  return 0; }\n"
    )
    c = tmp_path / "angle.c"
    c.write_text(program)
    exe = tmp_path / "angle"
    subprocess.run(["cc", "-o", str(exe), str(c)], check=True)
    return subprocess.run(
        [str(exe)], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True
    ).stdout


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
def test_patched_first_angle_is_a_number(tmp_path):
    patched = kp.guard_the_zero_count(UPSTREAM.read_text())
    assert _first_angle_at_count_zero(tmp_path, patched) == "0.000000"


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
def test_upstream_first_angle_is_not_a_number(tmp_path):
    assert "nan" in _first_angle_at_count_zero(tmp_path, UPSTREAM.read_text()).lower()
EOF

content.text:
Entire Address Findings:

The one open finding is fixed and marked resolved on trail 83. Nothing is committed.

**Resolved via manual edit** (no suggested patch): the Kaleidocycle first frame divides 0 by 0 (`kaleidocycle.c:486`, medium).

- **Cause:** the reviewer was right. The hack starts with `bp->count = 0`, so a piece's angle `(i/2) * 4 * 180 / bp->count` is 0/0 on the first frame. The NaN reaches TinyGL's viewport conversion and is cast to an int, which is undefined behaviour.
- **Reproduced first:** a dump build with `-fsanitize=float-cast-overflow` reported "nan is outside the range of representable values of type 'int'" at `tinygl/src/vertex.c:139` on the first frame.
- **Fix:** `tools/kaleidocycle_patch.py` guards the denominator, using 1 when the count is 0. `patch_float_literals.py` writes a patched copy to `generated/kaleidocycle_patched.c`. That copy has no float-literal pass, so it stays double precision. `kaleidocycle_gl.c` includes the patched copy, and the vendored hack stays byte-identical.
- **After:** the same sanitizer build now runs 200 frames with no error.
- **Test:** `tools/tests/test_kaleidocycle_patch.py` compiles the hack's own `glRotatef` call at count 0. Upstream gives NaN and the patched version gives 0. Breaking the guard is caught.
- **Checks:** `test_hacks` passes (140 of 140) and the tools tests pass (620). The device build compiles at 58.8% of the flash partition. The frame pins didn't move, since only the first frame's NaN changed.
- **Docs:** I added a note to `.claude/rules/hacks.md`, including the sanitizer command.
- **Board:** I didn't flash it, since the change only affects a frame whose output was already garbage.

**Changed files:** `.claude/rules/hacks.md`, `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, `firmware/src/hacks/kaleidocycle_gl.c`, plus the new `tools/kaleidocycle_patch.py` and `tools/tests/test_kaleidocycle_patch.py`.

The reviews keep finding out-of-range reads and NaNs in the unmodified upstream code. If you'd like, I can sweep the other new hacks with the same sanitizer (and bounds checking) in one pass, so the next review round doesn't turn up more of them one at a time.

Want me to commit and push these to #139?
